title: “Peak Greenwashing”: Two Bills in Congress Endorse Misleading Recycling Claims
author: Lisa Song
content:
The plastics industry [spent decades convincing
consumers](https://www.npr.org/2020/09/11/897692090/how-big-oil-misled-the-
public-into-believing-plastic-would-be-recycled) that throwing used products
stamped with the “chasing arrows” symbol into a curbside bin meant they would
be recycled.

Now, amid growing awareness that many of those items never get reprocessed,
the industry is championing a pair of proposals in Congress that would give
misleading recycling claims the support of federal law.

On the surface, the two bipartisan House bills promise transparency for
consumers by establishing national standards for recycling and recycled
content labels.

But the legislation — promoted by oil, chemical and packaging companies that
spend millions of dollars lobbying Congress each year — would forbid states
from setting stricter requirements. That would neutralize efforts like
California’s “truth in labeling” law, which bans the chasing arrow symbol on
plastic products that contain toxic chemicals or that can’t realistically be
recycled.

One of the measures would endorse a controversial form of “mass balance”
accounting that allows companies to claim a product contains recycled content
when virtually none of it came from reprocessed plastic. Two years ago, [a
ProPublica investigation](https://www.propublica.org/article/delusion-
advanced-chemical-plastic-recycling-pyrolysis) exposed the misleading,
mathematical sleight of hand used in that type of mass balance, which [the
Biden administration subsequently
prohibited](https://www.propublica.org/article/epa-rejects-mass-balance-
plastics-recycling-safer-choice) for specific products.

Both bills, which have gained momentum and could face a full House vote after
the midterm elections, “are peak greenwashing,” Rachel Fullmer, a staff
attorney on toxics and environmental health at the Natural Resources Defense
Council, said in an email. They “champion deceptive, anti-consumer policies
which would result in an increase in plastic production and plastic waste
incineration, all while hiding behind the false brand of ‘recycling.’”

Experts say the best solution to the plastics crisis wreaking havoc on human
health and the environment is to make and use less of the material; recycling
remains a marginal solution at best.

The bills tackle a growing threat to the industry, as several states have
proposed or passed laws that require manufacturers to more honestly
acknowledge the challenges of recycling plastic. Those measures could force
companies to spend money changing their packaging or labels.

The [Consumer Brands
Association](https://consumerbrandsassociation.org/letter/support-of-rmaa-and-
pack-act/), which represents the packaged goods industry including Amazon,
PepsiCo and Land O’Lakes, praised the House bills.

These proposals “work in tandem to reduce consumer confusion and plastic waste
while providing much-needed clarity to support new domestic innovations and
investments,” [the organization
wrote](https://consumerbrandsassociation.org/letter/support-of-rmaa-and-pack-
act/) to the leaders of the House Energy and Commerce Committee in July. They
“demonstrate that consumer protection and recycling-focused efforts go hand-
in-hand with promoting affordability and manufacturing investments, and we
strongly encourage your support for both bills.”  

The association spent $2.4 million in the first half of 2026 [lobbying on
these bills and other issues](https://www.opensecrets.org/federal-
lobbying/clients/consumer-brands-assn/reports?client_id=152647&cycle=2026),
according to data from OpenSecrets. In September, the two recycling bills
cleared the House committee.

Five Democratic House members, including three from Texas, are among the 13
co-sponsors of the [bill that endorses mass balance
accounting](https://www.congress.gov/bill/119th-congress/house-bill/7502). The
[other has 19 co-sponsors](https://www.congress.gov/bill/119th-congress/house-
bill/6832), including one Democrat.

A few weeks ago, Sen. John Curtis, a Utah Republican, introduced the [mass
balance bill in the Senate](https://www.congress.gov/bill/119th-
congress/senate-bill/5674/text?s=4&r=1); it currently has no other co-
sponsors.

### Sheen of Recyclability

Consumers have long been confused by the chasing arrows symbol on many plastic
containers. The label was created in 1970 to encourage paper recycling. The
plastics industry began placing it on its products in the 1980s [to quell
public outrage over plastic pollution](https://grist.org/culture/recycling-
symbol-logo-plastic-design/).

The symbol gave plastic the sheen of recyclability, even though most items
cannot be reprocessed due to economic or technical barriers. The
[Environmental Protection Agency estimated](https://www.epa.gov/facts-and-
figures-about-materials-waste-and-recycling/plastics-material-specific-data)
that 8.7% of U.S. plastic waste was recycled in 2018; the rest ended up in
landfills or was incinerated. In 2019, [the Department of
Energy](https://www.globenewswire.com/news-
release/2022/04/28/2431659/0/en/NREL-Calculates-Lost-Value-of-Landfilled-
Plastic-in-U-S.html) estimated the national plastic recycling rate at 5%.

In recent years, the plastics industry has touted the promise of chemical
recycling, a set of costly, often polluting technologies that break plastic
into its molecular building blocks. Theoretically, these processes could take
the most stubborn, unrecyclable plastics, like grocery store bags or string
cheese wrappers, and rebuild them into new products.

That rarely happens.

Take ExxonMobil’s chemical recycling plant in Baytown, Texas. It uses oil
refinery equipment to heat up the plastic and transform it into different
chemical compounds.

Lee Zeldin, the EPA administrator, [visited the Baytown plant last
year](https://www.eenews.net/articles/zeldin-touts-limitless-potential-for-
chemical-recycling/). He later appeared in [a promotional
video](https://corporate.exxonmobil.com/news/corporate-news/epa-administrator-
lee-zeldin-tours-our-advanced-recycling-operations-in-
baytown#Videoofthevisit), calling the facility a “proof of concept” for
chemical recycling that could inspire “this entire country.”

But only 8% of the plastic waste processed by ExxonMobil gets transformed into
new plastic, [according to the California attorney general’s
office](https://www.propublica.org/article/exxonmobil-plastics-recycling-
pyrolysis-lawsuit-california), which [sued the company in
2024](https://oag.ca.gov/system/files/attachments/press-
docs/Complaint_People%20v.%20Exxon%20Mobil%20et%20al.pdf) over “deceptively”
promoting chemical recycling as an environmental solution. The other 92%
mostly becomes fuel, which is burned rather than made into plastic products.

Citing internal company records, the lawsuit states that the recycled plastic
is so heavily diluted with new plastic, the resulting products contain less
than 0.1% recycled content.

In response, [the company
said](https://storage.courtlistener.com/recap/gov.uscourts.cand.438710/gov.uscourts.cand.438710.21.0.pdf)
in a court filing that while the state of California may not believe
ExxonMobil’s recycling technologies are sufficient to solve the plastic waste
crisis, “ExxonMobil did not assume liability for global pollution by
innovating solutions to the problem.”

The company has marketed its chemically recycled products as containing “30%
ISCC PLUS certified-circular” content, a technical term that could easily be
misinterpreted as meaning 30% recycled material. That label is possible
through a specific type of [mass balance, which allows companies
to](https://www.propublica.org/article/delusion-advanced-chemical-plastic-
recycling-pyrolysis) claim credit in a new plastic product for the recycled
molecules going into other things made in the chemical recycling process.
Manufacturers can inflate the reported recycledness, or “circularity,” of the
more lucrative products like plastic, while reducing the advertised recycled
content of less valuable products.

The Recycled Materials Attribution Act, introduced by Rep. Nick Langworthy, a
New York Republican, would require the Federal Trade Commission to edit the
Green Guides — advertising guidelines designed to prevent greenwashing — so
mass balance is recognized as “an acceptable method for substantiating
recycled content claims.”

It would bypass the FTC’s own process for revising the Green Guides, which
began several years ago. The agency had [collected more than 1,000 public
comments](https://www.regulations.gov/docket/FTC-2022-0077/comments),
including ones on whether limits should be placed on mass balance.

The bill also prevents states from adopting stricter laws on mass balance.

The Recycling Leadership Council is an industry consortium supporting
Langworthy’s bill. The consortium quoted Langworthy in its [February press
release](https://www.recyclingleadershipcouncil.org/news/introduction-of-the-
recycled-materials-attribution-act), touting the legislation as modernizing
recycling guidelines “with a uniform national standard that protects consumers
from misleading claims while giving American manufacturers the certainty they
need to invest, innovate, and compete.”

In the first half of this year, the council spent $120,000 [lobbying for
Langworthy’s
bill](https://lda.gov/filings/public/filing/7ccf7682-51f2-41fe-863e-150f1db16572/print/)
and related issues, including [“advanced
recycling](https://lda.gov/filings/public/filing/bd399dc6-813e-467e-8500-81f00b9efd77/print/)”
— the industry’s preferred term for chemical recycling.

“Advanced recycling technologies offer an important opportunity to keep more
plastic waste out of landfills,” John Hewitt, spokesperson for the Recycling
Leadership Council, said in an email.

Hewitt, who also represents the Consumer Brands Association, cited a [report
from a center-left think tank](https://www.progressivepolicy.org/the-waste-
diversion-benefits-of-expanding-advanced-recycling/), which concluded that
investing in chemical recycling could more than double the U.S. plastic
recycling rate.

Hewitt also defended the bill’s endorsement of mass balance, which “is an
established method for tracking recycled materials through complex
manufacturing processes, allowing companies to incorporate more recycled
content into products.”

Chemical recycling has [struggled to operate at
scale](https://www.nytimes.com/2026/07/09/climate/advanced-recycling.html). If
the mass balance bill passes, it could help ExxonMobil and other companies
grow their business, as consumers are willing to pay a premium for sustainable
products.

![A man wearing a suit and tie sits at a wooden table with a microphone. His
reflection can be seen in the table under him.](https://www.propublica.org/wp-
content/uploads/2026/10/GettyImages-2203485231.jpg?w=2560)Rep. Nick Langworthy
introduced the Recycled Materials Attribution Act, which would allow companies
to use mass balance accounting to drastically increase the advertised recycled
content in plastic products. Kayla Bartkowski/Getty Images

[ExxonMobil spent more than $5 million](https://www.opensecrets.org/federal-
lobbying/bills/hr7502?bill_id=hr7502-119) in the first half of 2026 lobbying
on the mass balance bill and many other energy or environmental issues. The
company didn’t return requests for comment.

Langworthy’s campaign committee received [$157,000 from the energy
sector](https://www.opensecrets.org/profiles/nick-
langworthy/us_congress/industries?mpid=1152109&cycle=2026&display=candidate&Select+cycle=2026)
in the 2026 election cycle, including oil and gas producers and chemical
companies. He did not respond to requests for comment.

### Bound for a Landfill

The other bill, the Packaging and Claims Knowledge (PACK) Act, would regulate
which items can be marketed as recyclable, compostable or reusable. Consumer
product packaging could only be stamped with the chasing arrows recycling
symbol if at least 60% of consumers have access to recycling programs that
accept the product. The item must also be technically recyclable, meaning it
“can be” reprocessed into a new product — but there’s no requirement to show
it’s economically feasible to do so.

[Recycling programs sometimes accept plastic
products](https://grist.org/accountability/inside-the-industry-push-to-label-
your-yogurt-cup-recyclable/) even when there’s no affordable way to ship them
to a factory that will make them into something new; as a result, plastic
that’s been collected for recycling ends up in a landfill or incinerator.

Products not meeting the 60% criteria must include qualifying language, such
as “check locally” to see if it’s accepted for recycling.

The bill, introduced by Rep. Randy Weber, a Texas Republican, targets states
like California that have stronger requirements for the chasing arrows symbol.
A recent California law requires 60% of Californians to have access to
facilities that routinely collect, sort and sell the products for
reprocessing. In addition, products will be disqualified if they have inks or
labels that prevent recycling, or if they contain certain levels of heavy
metals and the “forever chemicals” known as PFAS, some of which are
carcinogenic.

When Weber introduced the bill last December, [his press release called out
California’s
law](https://weber.house.gov/news/documentsingle.aspx?DocumentID=3542):
“Packaging and labeling standards in the United States are increasingly
influenced by state-level regulations, particularly those adopted in
California.”

“The PACK Act cuts through that confusion,” he said in the press release.
“It’s pro-environment, pro-business, and rooted in common sense.”

Weber did not return calls for comment. His campaign committee has [received
$206,000 from the energy sector and chemical
companies](https://www.opensecrets.org/profiles/randy-
weber/us_congress/industries?mpid=1149364&cycle=2026&display=candidate&Select+cycle=2026)
during the 2026 election cycle.

The bill provides little detail about who will make the crucial decisions on
which products qualify or what data will be used.

But at least some power will be given to unspecified “accredited third-party
certification” groups, which will certify every product’s recyclability claim.
These nominally independent organizations provide sustainability labels for
various companies.

One example of such a group is How2Recycle, which provides recycling labels —
for a fee — to companies. The labels are meant to erase consumer confusion, by
instructing them to “empty and replace cap” before recycling a particular kind
of bottle, for instance.

These third-party groups are supposed to be independent, but they’re easily
captured by industry interests, said Kate O’Neill, an environmental science
professor at the University of California-Berkeley who specializes in the
politics of recycling.

How2Recycle’s parent organization, the [Sustainable Packaging
Coalition](https://sustainablepackaging.org/membership-directory/), has a
membership dominated by retailers, brands and packaging companies. Members
include Google, Chobani, 3M, Clorox and Lego. (The EPA and United States
Postal Service are also members.) Several years ago, How2Recycle [made the
questionable claim that No. 5
plastics](https://grist.org/accountability/inside-the-industry-push-to-label-
your-yogurt-cup-recyclable/), used in yogurt tubs, were widely accepted for
recycling.

How2Recycle and the Sustainable Packaging Coalition didn’t return requests for
comment before publication.

California’s law is under a preliminary injunction due to a lawsuit from food
producers and packaging companies. However, consumers can still bring private
lawsuits if they suspect companies of falsely using the recycling symbol on
their products, Lynn Dyer, president of the packaging trade group Ameripen,
said in an email.

“AMERIPEN recognized early that differing state rules could make it harder for
businesses to explain how consumers should handle packaging after use,” Dyer
said. So Ameripen brought together a coalition and “helped make the case to
Congress,” resulting in Weber’s bill. The group has “been engaged in
discussions with congressional staff from the outset, have closely followed
the bill’s development, and draw on the experience of organizations across the
packaging value chain.”

In July, Ameripen [urged manufacturers, retailers and brands to tell their
members of
Congress](https://members.ameripen.org/theameripenvoice/Details/take-action-
help-advance-the-pack-act-to-establish-consistent-national-packaging-
labeling-344250) to back the bill. Ameripen spent $160,000 lobbying for the
legislation and other environmental issues from January to June 2026.

ProPublica reached out to every co-sponsor of the House bills. Rep. Earl L.
“Buddy” Carter, a Republican from Georgia who supports the PACK Act, was the
only lawmaker who responded.

“American consumers deserve clear, consistent, and reliable information about
the products they purchase, and our manufacturers deserve a predictable set of
rules to follow,” Carter said in a statement. “The PACK Act is about
establishing a uniform national standard that eliminates confusion, supports
American manufacturing, and provides greater certainty for businesses and
consumers alike. We can promote responsible recycling practices without
forcing American businesses to navigate a patchwork of conflicting state
regulations.”
